content: H1N2 is a subtype of the Influenza A virus, which is sometimes referred to as the bird flu virus. This particular subtype is currently endemic in both human and pig populations. Among the Influenza A virus subtypes, H1N1, H1N2, and H3N2 are the only ones known to be actively circulating in humans at present. The emergence of the A(H1N2) strain is believed to have occurred due to a reassortment of genetic material between the currently circulating A(H1N1) and A(H3N2) subtypes. Specifically, the hemagglutinin (H) protein of the A(H1N2) virus closely resembles that of the A(H1N1) viruses, while the neuraminidase (N) protein is similar to that of the A(H3N2) viruses. However, the exact origin of the A(H1N2) virus remains unknown. On February 6, 2002, the World Health Organization (WHO) in Geneva, along with the Public Health Laboratory Service (PHLS) in the United Kingdom, reported the identification of the A(H1N2) virus in human cases from England, Israel, and Egypt. Additionally, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) identified the A(H1N2) virus in patient samples collected during the 2001-2002 and 2002-2003 influenza seasons. Historically, A(H1N2) viruses have circulated briefly in the past. For example, between December 1988 and March 1989, 19 isolates of the A(H1N2) virus were identified in six cities in China. However, the virus did not spread further at that time. The H1N2 virus is not significantly different from the influenza viruses currently circulating. The H1 protein of the H1N2 virus is similar to the H1 protein found in the A(H1N1) viruses, and the N2 protein is comparable to the N2 protein in the A(H3N2) viruses. What is unusual is the combination of the H1 and N2 proteins on the same virus, as this is not commonly observed. Importantly, the A(H1N2) virus is not associated with causing more severe illness compared to other influenza viruses. No unusual increases in influenza activity have been linked to the A(H1N2) virus. Furthermore, because the hemagglutinin and neuraminidase proteins of the A(H1N2) virus closely match those of the viruses included in the current influenza vaccine, the vaccine is expected to provide effective protection against the A(H1N2) virus. It also continues to offer protection against the currently circulating A(H1N1), A(H3N2), and influenza B viruses.
